subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in this debate and to lend my support to the amendment which has been put forward. In reading through the Bill, I am somewhat surprised if not annoyed that the Conservative Government would put such a Bill before the Parliament of Canada. In fact, when government Members were on this side of the House, they argued for a considerable amount of time to the effect that when borrowing Bills come before Parliament, they ought to be clear.
Part I of this particular Bill requests a certain sum of money and Part II requests an additional sum of money. Part II of the Bill is not clear. It is not clear why that money is being requested. In fact, there has been no budget although it could be argued that the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was in fact a mini-budget. However, the Government has chosen to call it an economic statement and not a budget.
The Government is now asking the Parliament of Canada to approve expenditures which are in the billions of dollars, including approximately $16 billion for fiscal year 1985-86. However, we have yet to learn what it wants to spend that money on.
Government Members said during the election campaign that their major priority was jobs. Unfortunately for the 1.5 million unemployed Canadians, the rhetoric that was used during the campaign has not been put into action either in the Throne Speech or indeed in the economic statement. Instead,
we have seen a great many economic cuts affecting all areas of Canada and particularly the poorer regions of Canada.
I find it to be a bit hypocritical, if you will, Mr. Speaker, for Conservative Members who are now in a position of power to say to the people of Canada: "We want $16 billion but we are not going to tell you what we are going to do with it". They are not telling us what they are going to do with it with regard to employment and employment opportunities. We have heard the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) talk about an economic employment strategy, and indeed that strategy was alluded to by the Minister of Finance. Yet we have not seen any signs to tell us what it will comprise.
Government Members have not put before Parliament any measures that would be of some assistance to young Canadians. They have not put any package of legislation before the House to assist women or minority groups with regard to employment opportunities. What are they prepared to do with the $16 billion that they are requesting from Parliament?
Perhaps the argument can be made that the money they are requesting is not going to be directed toward job creation or social programs. Perhaps it will be directed toward the private sector by providing more tax concessions to businesses. In theory, there is nothing wrong with tax incentives and with providing financial assistance to private sector companies which, we would hope, would create employment.
[DOT] (mo)
Just yesterday, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association released a survey which indicated that for the month of October production had decreased substantially and unemployment had increased. The private sector, as alluded to by the Government, will not resolve unilaterally all the evils of unemployment. Government must assist. Government must be an active player. We have received the complete opposite from this Government.
There used to be some red Tories, but they have been overcome by the blue tidal wave. What has happened is that programs which were in place for young people, such as the Canada student employment program, have been cancelled. We have a Government which said that consultation was the key, operative word. Were young people consulted with regard to the cancellation of the Canada student employment program? Absolutely not.
The Government talks about consultation. Then it unilaterally moves to cut the deficit by $4.2 billion-and many of those cuts will affect the less fortunate in the country-and indicates that it will study further how the deficit can be reduced, whether by reductions in terms of tax reform, tax incentives or the curtailment of social programs. Yet it has the

December 6, 1984
Borrowing Authority
audacity to say to Canadians that it is trying to improve investor confidence. That is absolute nonsense. Will investors invest if there is going to be consultation, when the Government unilaterally cuts $4.2 billion and then says that it will have further studies? I suggest that the business community in Canada and abroad will wait until well after a federal Budget is announced. So much for confidence in the private sector. The private sector will wait to see what is the outcome of those discussions. They will wait to see what tax incentives are put in place. They will want to know what the effects of those incentives will be for them as business individuals.
We have a Government which speaks of confidence, but in actual fact it is not restoring confidence. It has increased the lack of confidence by the measures which it has placed before Parliament. I find it very difficult to accept that some of the red Tories who were on this side and who are now in government are allowing the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), "Mike the Knife"-the Minister of Finance-and all the right-wingers in the Government to override completely any interests of and concerns for the less fortunate in Canada.
Members opposite laugh, but the 1.5 million unemployed Canadians are not laughing. Statistics Canada has reported that 600,000 young people are unemployed. Three hundred thousand unemployed have given up their desire to look for employment because there are no jobs. It is a human tragedy and this Government has done absolutely nothing to assist. The Government has aided and abetted this tragedy by doing nothing for these people. Instead it has taken direct action to affect those individuals who are the least fortunate in our society.
I would like to know what portion of the $16 billion will be directed towards direct job-creation programs in this country. How much money will be put into the training of young people, women and minority groups in this country? How much money will be put into regional industrial development? The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion has reduced its budget by $200 million. I will break it down into tier one, the so-called more fortunate area, as opposed to tier four, the less fortunate areas. Tier four has been reduced by 25 per cent whereas tier one has been reduced by 16 per cent. That, Mr. Speaker, is Tory justice.
This Government has an obligation to place before Parliament information which is not readily available to this Parliament but is readily available to it. I very strongly urge Members of the Government to rise in their places and represent their constituents, not the view which has been expounded by the right-wingers, whether they come from Toronto or Washington. This is a Reagan economic policy, Mr. Speaker, which should be abandoned. Parliament ought to have that information before it approves a $16 billion commitment to this Government.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to speak against the motion of the Government which asks for borrowing authority from this House. The Bill has two parts. It asks for $5.3 billion to cover expenditures which the Government foresees between now and the end of the fiscal year, and it requests an extra $2 billion in case the Government has miscalculated its contingency fund. The Bill further asks for $16 billion for expenditures the Government proposes to make after March 31, 1985.
The point has been made many times about the change in attitude which Members of the Government have now as opposed to the time when they were the Opposition. I can recall the days and days of debate when those Hon. Members would berate the Liberal government for attempting to ask for money from Parliament when the Liberal government had not given the House any indication of how it was intending to spend the money.
Borrowing Authority
We have not had a budget, nor have we had any indication of what the money will be used for after March 31. We believe that the $16 billion is totally uncalled for. We realize that governments from time to time need money because taxes do not come in as fast as expenditures. We are aware that the Government is carrying a deficit somewhere between $30 billion and $35 billion. Most of that deficit it inherited, but it has done very little about it.
The economic statement addressed only the reduction of expenditures. The response to those proposals in the business community seems to have been negative. While they were enthusiastic about the support of cut-backs in the press, when business associations began to survey their memberships they found that they were less optimistic about the future than they were several months ago. The result has been negative. I think it is time the Government began to look elsewhere for solutions to get the economy going.
I would bring to the attention of the Government the positive program which we presented to the electorate in the last election. The electorate in 30 ridings paid some attention to our program. I will reiterate that program, because I do not think Members opposite paid much attention to it. During the election campaign virtually all of our program was eventually picked up by Conservative candidates, with two notable exceptions. I think the key to turning the economy around lies with those two exceptions. One was a made-in-Canada interest policy. That policy would recognize that the Government of Canada does have control over the Bank of Canada, that it sets the guidelines for the economy of the country, and that it can operate an economy which is separate from that of the United States. We attempted to make that point many times during the campaign, but it was not as well picked up as it might have been so I will repeat it now.
First, Canada is not like the United States. Canada has a positive trade balance and has had a very sizeable balance of trade for the past five or six years. Unlike the United States, Canada has a positive savings balance. Canadians save more money than they invest. There are plenty of funds generated within Canada. We do not have to build up interest rates in order to attract outside investment, because there is a surplus of investment funds created here annually. That is quite different from the United States which spends more money in investments than it generates. People in the United States are not good savers and never have been. They do not generate enough funds from within their own territory to meet their investment needs. Canada is quite different. It makes no sense to adopt policies that are consistent with those in the United States. A point that is often overlooked is that Canadian workers are more efficient than American workers. During the last two years worker productivity in Canada has outstripped worker productivity in the United States.
Those are three basic economic indicators which tell us that Canada is a very strong country. Canada has a good basis for beginning an upsurge in the economy. The one thing which is holding it back is our high, restrictive over-burdening interest rates. No consumer is going to increase his purchasing as long

December 6, 1984
Borrowing Authority
as those interest rates stay high. Home owners are going to be very careful about buying houses. Farmers and small business are going to be very cautious about making future investments. All of those things are absolutely necessary if we are going to get the economy growing and find employment for the 11 per cent of our population who want to work but have no jobs.
The second item which was discussed during the election campaign but is not now being mentioned by the Conservatives who make up the Government is the necessity for a fair taxation system. We recognize that small business is the engine of growth in this country, unlike the United States which relies more heavily on big business. More than 70 per cent of the new jobs created last year were created by small business, so it is vital that the tax system works well for small business.
Because of the shortcomings in the proposal which is before us, Mr. Speaker, I would like to introduce an amendment to the motion. I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin):
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and the following substituted therefor:
"Bill C-11, an Act to provide borrowing authority, be not now read a second
time but that it be read a second time this day six months hence".

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak in this important moment in the history of the House of Commons. I want to take this opportunity to speak on the amendment to Bill C-l 1, an Act to provide borrowing authority. Perhaps the obvious reason for the amendment being put before the House this morning is that this borrowing authority covers more than a one-year period. In fact, it provides over $7 billion of borrowing authority for the next four and a half months of this fiscal year and then provides another $16 billion for the 1985-86 fiscal year.
The Government came to power on a policy of creating jobs and economic activity and suddenly, after it has achieved power, it has changed direction and its overriding preoccupation now is with reducing the deficit. We really do not know what the Government's spending plans to create the economic activity which the Conservatives talked about so much in the past will be. We have not heard any definite plans spelled out as to exactly how this $16 billion plus $7 billion will be spent.
The Bill looks ahead not only to the end of this fiscal year but into the following fiscal year, so we are really considering a period of some 17 or 18 months into the future. The obvious question is, why should Hon. Members on this side of the House, or Hon. Members on the other side, buy a pig in a poke for what amounts to two fiscal years? We must ask ourselves, is the Government really trying to be secretive about this? The marching orders went out as soon as the Cabinet was sworn in on September 18 to hold everything in confidence and to keep everything secret. Soon the edict went out from the Secretary
of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) that people in his Department were not to talk to the press or to Members of Parliament or to anyone else, socially or otherwise. That edict has been withdrawn but there certainly is still a permeating idea of secrecy which follows right through to Bill C-ll which is before us today.
We really do not know what the Government is going to spend this money on, Mr. Speaker. The cost of ministerial staff has been increased by $140,000 to $400,000 for each Minister. We do not know whether that amount will be increased even more. Perhaps there will be appointed a second chief of staff, in a way similar to American politics. The Cabinet will be further bloated from last summer where there were 29 Ministers of the former Government to 40 Ministers of the present Government. When we leave the House of Commons at night we see those 40 Oldsmobile 98s sitting out in front with their two-way radios and chauffeurs. We do not know whether there is going to be more spending like that.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) did us a favour last week, he said, when he told us that the Department of Public Works actually wanted to spend $600,000 on 24 Sussex Drive and he talked them down to $100,000. Although in his view, he has saved us $500,000, we really have to question whether or not some of this $16 billion will be spent on those kinds of things.
The Prime Minister indicated that he is going to pay for his own hot tub and the television satellite dish for his Harrington Lake residence. He also told us last summer that the Parliament of Canada was not going to have to pay for his nanny. However, it developed that we were going to have to pay for the nanny. Further inquiries were made and it was said that the nanny really was not the nanny any longer, she was a maid. When asked about that the explanation was that she was a maid, but a maid who interfaces on a continuing basis with the children. Obviously, sometimes these terms can be switched around. We just wonder whether some part of these funds will ultimately go towards the cost of the hot tub and the television dish. Perhaps the Prime Minister will invoke that prime ministerial provision as he did with the Government JetStars when he was questioned about whether they were being used by Ministers for personal use. He said in a deep voice that they were really sacred instruments of government travel. I can just imagine that if the Government of Canada ends up paying for the hot tub and the television dish, the Prime Minister will probably use his deepest prime ministerial tones at the press conference and say that they are sacred instruments for prime ministerial comfort and titillation.
In any case we have this Bill for borrowing authority of $7 billion for this fiscal year and $16 billion for the coming fiscal year before us. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the difficulty for this Government is that it came to power with many, many promises which it knew, and we knew, and now everyone knows, could not be kept. Instead of going ahead and implementing those promises on an orderly basis, it wants to switch them over to the standing committees of the House or have
December 6, 1984

consultation with other groups outside the House and we really do not know where the Government is going.
We have in Bill C-7 legislation to implement the tax proposals of the previous government. This Government has brought in legislation from the previous Parliament but it does not seem to want to bring in even the uncontroversial legislation of its own. When a Party gets 211 seats in Parliament it should be able to see that its campaign promises are implemented. There were solemn promises concerning agriculture. Legislation and funding would be provided so that outstanding farm loans, a tremendous handicap to our agricultural producers at interest rates of 16 per cent and 17 per cent, would be written down to current day interest rates. Yet there is no legislation to implement that promise. There is no legislation to implement set-asides such as was done in the United States, or to bring back the special farm financing assistance program of the previous government.
In his economic statement the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) spelled out in pretty good detail what this Government is against, but what we do not know and what this Bill does not provide is which promises made during the election campaign the Government is going to keep. That is why I think the Official Opposition, at least, would like to see this Bill split into two parts, one for this fiscal year and one for the next fiscal year.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak to this Bill, the objectionable part of which says that we are to borrow $16 billion for the year 1985-86 without having any budget in front of us whatsoever. We objected to this from the beginning. The earlier amendment proposed a much more direct sort of remedy, namely simply to split it. We offered that option to the Government. One or two government Members asked us, rhetorically as it were, whether we would accept such a split and we said quite clearly yes, we would. However, there was obviously no move from the government side to consider such a split although that was exactly what the Conservatives asked for and got two years ago when the shoe was on the other foot and they were sitting on the other side of the Speaker.
Therefore, we are asking for a six-month hoist which will give the Government time to do its arithmetic and determine what it wants to use the money for. This is the tradition of Parliament in Britain and Canada. The control of spending by Parliament has been a fundamental cause for which parliamentarians lived and died, and for which a king of England lost his head. He insisted on spending money without authority so they chopped off the head of Charles I. We are not proposing anything so drastic as that, Mr. Speaker. I see the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) looking a little anxious! I can assure him we would not want to do anything more over this motion than defeat the Government and have an election.

He would still have his head. We did not do that while I was here, Mr. Speaker, and I would still like to see it.
We really have to oppose this motion. This is the policy that R. B. Bennett tried and which proved utterly disastrous half a century ago. It was a policy of trying to cure a depression by forcing unemployment. What he did was to double the depression; it did not last five years, it lasted 10 years, thanks to R. B. Bennett's policy. Unfortunately, memories are short and apparently members of the Government have not read their Canadian history or talked to their parents about the depression. They do not know that they are doing exactly the same thing that turned a disaster into a double disaster half a century ago.
There have been warnings from financial authorities that even if there has been a short spurt to the economy through international trade, the domestic economy is not picking up. It remains flat. In fact, the spurt in international trade may be turning down again. I wish the members of the Government would heed that warning because their policies failed in the view of ordinary people as well as in the view of economists.
For example, the Government has decided to wipe out 4,000 jobs in the home building industry by cutting $9.6 million from the social housing budget. The subsidy for a unit is in the range of $5,000. Roughly speaking, that will cut out about 1,900 units and about 4,000 jobs in construction and home furnishings. It is accepted in the building trade that each unit means about one job in construction and a little more than one job per year in home furnishings. By cutting $9.6 million from the social housing budget, the Government is wiping out 4,000 jobs when unemployment is already too high. The Government says: Don't worry, just stop eating or tell your constituents to stop eating and probably in a year some more jobs will appear from somewhere when the economy has been stimulated and confidence is restored. In the meantime, confidence is going down the drain and the Government is taking bread and butter off the table of many working people.
This Government is not increasing confidence, Mr. Speaker. Reports of economists show that. The Government has taken another $29.4 million from rehabilitation, probably another 600 jobs. Then there is the money cut from insulation programs. More jobs lost. These are labour-intensive programs which employ people in the cities of Canada where the unemployed are mostly congregated. Those are jobs that could employ people who have known skills. They do not need a retraining program, they are ready to go to work today. But the Government has cut them off. Not only those families suffer, but the tradesmen and merchants who would like to sell to those families suffer as well because these people do not have money to buy the goods.
In the same way, Mr. Speaker, the Government is cutting back on all kinds of social programs. I want to speak particularly about the immigrant settlement adaptation program. The Government provides less than $400 per immigrant for the whole process of getting settled and learning English. That is a

Borrowing Authority
serious hindrance to their settlement in this country. The kind of cuts the Government is making in the budget do not give us any confidence that it will spend the money in the proper way in the coming year. If the Government would show us how it will spend the money, we would be able to decide whether that is what Parliament wants.
Until then, Mr. Speaker, we have to say that without any accounting or budgeting in advance it would be utterly improper for Parliament to vote the Government a blank cheque of $16 billion. That is equivalent to $1,000 or more for every family in Canada. We simply cannot afford to put that money in the hands of untried people who refuse to give us any budget or account.
I would hope that Hon. Members on both sides of the House will consider very seriously the danger of what the Government proposes to do and will support this very sensible and conservative motion that has been put forward by our House Whip.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to be able to speak to the amendment on Bill C-ll, an Act to provide borrowing authority. To say that this Bill is nebulous gives a completely new definition to the word. We are asked to approve a Bill in two parts. The first part is for $7.3 billion for the fiscal year 1984-85. The second part is for $16 billion for the fiscal year 1985-86.
There are really two parts to the amount that we are being asked to approve for this year. The first part of the $7.3 billion relates to increased expenses of $5.3 billion. The second part is for a $2 billion reserve fund. I think it would be more commonly described as a slush fund.
Why are we being asked to approve this Bill at this particular time? It is mainly because of a statement that has been termed an economic and fiscal statement. It has certainly not been called a budget, yet we are asked in the House to approve this Bill giving authority to borrow a tremendous sum of money. We are asked to give the Government this money blindly on what is produced in that statement without having produced a budget or brought down estimates. Certainly it would be a travesty to the people of Canada, to the House and to Members of Parliament as representatives of the people of Canada to approve this sum of money with the sketchy information that has been provided.
Where is this money going to go? No one has been given any inkling of what the Government plans to do. Certainly the Government has not given us any information in its election promises. Any election promises that have been kept have been purely coincidental. What was said during the election campaign was for the consumption of the Canadian public to be used to forward that Party's platform for the election. It has become increasingly obvious that the Government had no intention of keeping those election promises.
Again I ask, where is this money going to go? What will be the benefit to the Canadian public? Where are the programs that the Government is supposed to have brought forward for the betterment of the Canadian public and the economy, which
we have agreed needs attention? Certainly the deficit is important and needs attention. However, what are people going to do, not only in the long-term, which has received some consideration, but in the short-term? How are people going to cope? How is the Government's program going to deal with this very important question? In its economic and fiscal statement the Government said that it is going to cut $200 million from regional development programs. There is nothing to indicate that the Government in any way has any feeling for the low income and unemployed Canadians, let alone any concept of how it is going to attack the very important problem of regional disparity and unemployment in the country. This is not only a lack of policy; it is insensitivity to this very important question.
Where is the energy policy that was promised? During the election campaign the Government Party was not shy in stating what it planned to do. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) admitted freely prior to the election campaign that she had consulted on various occasions with industry and consumer groups. I think it is paramount that we get some indication of what the energy policy is going to be before we approve this extremely large sum of money. I do not think it is unreasonable; I think it is very responsible and in the interests of the taxpayers of the country that we ask for this six-month extension to consider this Bill and the approval of this sum of money.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has said that she would like to use the energy policy as an engine for growth. If she does that, this certainly will involve a very considerable and substantial fiscal regime on the part of the Government. What is that fiscal regime going to be? Who is it going to benefit? Frankly, is it going to be sizeable at all and is it going to do what the Minister, the industry, and the people of the country are expecting it to do? We have no indication of this. The Minister herself has said that she cannot make major energy decisions until the world price of oil stabilizes. What is a stabilized world price for oil? Certainly the price has been stable for a month and that is about all anyone can expect from that category. Any conflict in the Middle East could have a tremendous impact on the world price of oil. That is no reason to postpone these major decisions on what the Government will do on this very important question.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) shed crocodile tears when he was Opposition about the needs of Canadians and the people who are disadvantaged. He is now prepared to jettison everything that previous governments have worked for to provide the best health care system in the country in the interest of trying to meet this blind desire to reduce expenditures. This strikes out at those who are the most defenceless in the country and the easiest targets of this blind economic policy which the Government is following. In addition to the blind economic policy, the Government is now asking us to grant this amount of money without our knowing to what use it will be put.
It would be irresponsible for the House to approve this Bill and this sum of money, Mr. Speaker. The Government is

December 6, 1984
irresponsible and not fulfilling its mandate even to table this Bill at this particular time in view of the sketchy information it has provided. The Government is not only acting irresponsibly, it is acting callously. I think that is a result of an elitist policy which has complete disregard for what Canadians are expecting from the mandate they have given to the Government.
I ask Members of all Parties to vote against this Bill and, particularly, to support the amendment to the Bill of my Party. Surely, with additional time the Government could come forward with at least some of the information we require for considering this Bill. In this six-month period it could at least go through the motions of informing Canadians how this money will be spent.
I submit that my Party has taken a very responsible position which is, frankly, a very moderate position in its amendment. We could have requested a good deal more from the Government in light of its arrogance in requesting the House to approve this Bill in its present form.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also rise on behalf of the people in my riding to call upon the Government to rethink its stand with respect to this Bill for at least the six-month period in question. I ask the Government to reconsider its current position with respect to the borrowing of billions of Canadian taxpayers' money without providing Parliament with the tools we need to carry out our job.
I know that there is extreme concern not only in my riding but in the community of Hamilton about the fulfilment of promises made by the Government, particularly those made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) with respect to the issue of steel import quotas. Members will no doubt be aware that during the election battles throughout the country we heard many flowery promises from the Prime Minister. In fact, he assured the people of my riding in a letter which he wrote to them that when he became Prime Minister he would do everything in his power to ensure that the Canadian steel market or the right of Canadian steel products to enter the United States was not infringed upon by quotas or other measures that would be in violation of GATT.
However, like so many other promises, the Prime Minister has disappointed and indeed disgusted the people of Hamilton East. I questioned the Prime Minister about this issue in the House earlier this week. His response was not one of a serious parliamentarian or head of state with respect to an issue of international importance and with international repercussions. Instead, it was a flip answer that was an attempt to castigate the present position taken by the Liberal Party that the Government must go to the President of the United States and insist that the labelling provisions which are a violation of GATT be withdrawn immediately or we will be prepared to take retaliatory measures.
The Prime Minister talked about retaliatory rhetoric. I want to inform the Prime Minister that there are hundreds of people in my riding and thousands throughout Hamilton who are
Borrowing Authority
facing a very bleak Christmas. Almost a thousand people have already been laid off. Some have received notice that they will be laid off by the end of January unless there is an upturn in steel production. One can imagine the kind of Christmas those constituents are awaiting. I rose in the House on behalf of those constituents of Hamilton East to ask the Prime Minister what stance the Government is prepared to take with respect to the negotiations with the Congress and the President of the United States. He simply replied with a laugh and a snarky rhetorical remark. Such a response by our Prime Minister to a serious question is not acceptable. It is not the kind of answer the people in my riding would have expected from the Prime Minister, particularly when they are facing serious job dislocation.
My colleagues and I have been extremely disappointed that the Government has chosen not to seize the opportunity it has been given as a result of its unprecedented mandate. Instead, it is spending most of its time raking the muck in search of stories and innuendos about the past history of former Liberal Ministers, including the current Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner).
I believe the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition said it best in Toronto last night when he asked if members of the Government did not realize that they have won the election and that, as of September 4, the Prime Minister and his Party was given a massive mandate by the people of Canada. Does he not realize that the election is over? He is no longer campaigning; he is in Parliament and the people of Canada are looking to him and the Government to provide leadership in the area of job creation and job protection.
As a Member who represents literally thousands of steel workers, I find it completely unacceptable for the Prime Minister to be unaware that the current tariff barriers being imposed by the U.S. Congress with respect to the labelling issue are a violation of GATT. Furthermore, he is unable to stand in his place in the House and tell Canadians that he is doing everything in his power to personally ensure the protection of Canadian steel jobs, as he promised during the election. While this issue is of particular importance to people in my riding, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) should also have a special interest in this issue. His constituents in Sault Ste. Marie are not looking to the Government for laughs and stand-up comicry; they are looking for leadership.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan), also spoke on this very serious issue. He is looking to the Government for leadership with respect to the steel industry in Nova Scotia. I find it unacceptable for the Government to ask for billions of dollars of unprecedented borrowing authority into the fiscal year of 1985-86 while the Prime Minister sloughs off such a serious question as the steel labelling issue.
When members of the Government are considering this amendment to delay the borrowing Bill for at least six months, they should recognize that they are also safeguarding their parliamentary privileges by insisting that the Prime Minister and the Cabinet come clean not only with Parliament but with

December 6, 1984
Borrowing Authority
their own caucus. For example, this is true with respect to Government decisions in such areas as CMHC. There is a very disturbing article on the front page of The Globe and Mail. The very existence of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation is at stake. At the same time, there is no action on the part of the Government or no attempt to inform Canadians that the Government's role in housing will not be wiped out as a result of its cost-cutting measures.
The people of Canada are frightened. They voted in the Government with a massive mandate for change. However, what they have received is government by secrecy, government by Cabinet and political commissar directives and government by centralization within the office of the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen).
I would venture to say that Conservative Members of the House will have just as much difficulty when they go to committee to seek information on issues which interest them and when they try to determine where the Government will make its cuts. At the moment there is a veil of uncertainty which is hanging over Canadians. It is hanging over the steel workers in Hamilton. It is hanging over single parents in Toronto who are trying to find adequate housing and, in some cases, wondering where they will get their next meal. This uncertainty is facing steel workers in Sydney.
I believe that these people would say that it is unacceptable comportment for the Prime Minister to laugh and slough off serious questions from the Opposition each day in Question Period. I believe that the people of Canada deserve more. The Government has been given a mandate and I plead with the Prime Minister to take a strong personal stand with respect to the steel labelling provision so that the steel workers of Hamilton can spend Christmas in the knowledge that their jobs will not be on the line.
It is a serious issue which should not be treated comically by the Government. It is an issue that affects the lives and economy not only of the steel workers but those in the automobile industry. These industries are interrelated and many sectors in our economy are waiting to see if the Prime Minister will provide leadership or simply scrape and bow to his American counterpart in the White House.

subsubtopic: USEFULNESS OF DETAILED DATA ON ETHNIC COMPOSITION OF POPULATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week at a sitting of the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, I pointed out to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) that cancelling the 1986 census would have a negative impact on our immigrants.
When the Minister replied that she failed to see how this cutback could be harmful, I suggested that she consult the principal users of StatsCan data, namely, our federal departments and agencies.
In fact, in a study ordered by StatsCan in 1982 to identify data requirements, principal users asked that collecting detailed data on ethnic non-native groups be maintained on a five-yearly basis, since the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms provides for the preservation and development of the multicultural heritage of Canadians. It is therefore official policy to help minority groups participate fully in the social, cultural and political life of this country.
Special programs exist for this purpose, and only the census can provide detailed information on the ethnic composition of the population.
The Minister would therefore do well to reconsider her position on the census.

Mr. Speaker, it is time Canadians got some answers from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) concerning his patronage appointments.
Last summer we saw an appalling rash of appointments requested by a retiring Mr. Trudeau being accepted by the new Liberal Leader (Mr. Turner) who said that "he had no option" but to accept Mr. Trudeau's wishes. The Conservative Leader lectured the Prime Minister of the day, saying: "You made those appointments and you have to bear the odious responsibility for them". We all know how dearly the Liberals paid for those pork barrel jobs. He added: "It would take the people of Manicouagan working until the end of their days to pay the salaries of those appointments".
Last July the Tory Leader said: "We are going to remove . . . patronage positions from automatic politics". Last August he said that a Conservative Government would submit appointments for key policy positions to a House committee
December 6, 1984

for review. It is now December and such a committee is nowhere in sight.
Now, it seems, the Prime Minister is playing the old Liberal game. He has recently begun to appoint loyalists and party "bag-men" to high-paying positions of public service. Since the people of Manicouagan are paying for the "Trudeau-Turner" pact, I wonder who the PM thinks will pay for his latest binge.
Prime Ministerial appointments must be reviewed by the House of Commons. In this new age of "accountable" government, I call on the Prime Minister to introduce immediately his proposal for such a review.

subtopic: CALL FOR AGRI-BOND PROGRAM AND FINANCIAL COUNSELLING SERVICES
CALL FOR AGRI-BOND PROGRAM AND FINANCIAL COUNSELLING SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of this House the serious financial crisis in agriculture. Canadian farmers are facing severe financial difficulty as a result of heavy debt loads, high interest rates, and low commodity and livestock prices. The drought last summer in western Canada has left many farmers with their backs to the wall. Across Canada the latest Farm Credit Corporation statistics indicate that 17 per cent of Canadian farmers are in severe financial stress, with a further 7 per cent under moderate stress.
I would urge my Government to make financial counselling services available to farmers to assist them in their negotiations with lending institutions, in order to arrange special repayment terms for viable farmers suffering temporary financial difficulties. This move would provide relief in the short term. I would further urge my Government to provide assistance in the long term by introducing an agri-bond program to provide long-term, low interest financing for the agricultural community.
With a famine situation throughout much of the Third World, I urge my Government to make financial assistance for the primary food producers in Canada and the preservation of the family farm a high priority item.

subtopic: REJECTION OF NATURAL GAS EXPORT PROPOSAL
REJECTION OF NATURAL GAS EXPORT PROPOSAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian economy has lost an infusion of $120 million. I refer to the recent National Energy Board decision rejecting the export of natural gas over a two-year period. The National Energy Board rejected this proposal because the price of the gas was less than the Toronto citygate price.
The proposed export at Emerson, Manitoba, is 1,200 miles closer to the source than Toronto. As an analogy, Mr. Speaker, if automobiles could not be exported from Oakville or from
Windsor at a price lower than the price in Winnipeg, not many, if any, would be exported.
We urge the Government to rescind this obsolete and ridiculous benchmark as soon as possible. This would give the ailing Canadian economy a much needed $120 million infusion, $120 million worth of jobs and taxes.

Mr. Speaker, the Government has been threatening and harassing public servants ever since it was sworn into office. Thousands of people are being laid off. The Government is breaking its promises to the general population, and especially to its public servants.
Not content with cutting jobs and creating havoc everywhere, it now appears that the Government will be increasing parking rates for public servants to an amount between $80 and $125 per month. Many government employees working at low wages are my constituents, who have to drive several miles to work using the inadequate Queensway, a courtesy of our provincial Tory Government, only to arrive on the job to be hit a double whammy by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and his friend, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle). Tory times are hard times, especially for our public servants, but they will remember this Government when the next election comes.

Mr. Speaker, over the course of the last few years, many Canadians have lost their homes as a result of very high interest rates. We noted with interest that neither the Conservative Party in opposition, nor the Liberal Party in government, was prepared to move to assist those individuals, and for them there was no abundant supply of public housing into which to move.
Since his election to the House of Commons the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has sold his home in Montreal for a handsome profit, and has moved three times from one public house into the next.
Just yesterday the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) chose to follow suit, selling his home in Toronto for a handsome profit, only to move into public housing, not the normal kind of public housing, public housing for which you pay no rent, public housing that requires absolutely no outlay on behalf of either of these gentlemen. When you weigh up what they have done over and against what happened to thousands of Canadians in the last five years, the question really is: Where is the justice?

December 6, 1984

maintopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION LONG DISTANCE TELEPHONE SERVICE APPLICATION-EFFECT ON SASKATCHEWAN RESIDENTS
CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION LONG DISTANCE TELEPHONE SERVICE APPLICATION-EFFECT ON SASKATCHEWAN RESIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a recent federal-provincial study shows that the Province of Saskatchewan would be the biggest loser if new companies are allowed to compete for long distance telephone service in Canada. According to the study, additional competition for long distance would drain off revenues and force the basic rates for local telephone service in rural Saskatchewan to triple in some areas.
Because of Saskatchewan's diverse land and relatively sparse population, our provincial phone company, Sask Tel, relies on long distance revenues to provide local phone service at reasonable rates. If this long distance revenue were to be lost, it might force hundreds of subscribers in Saskatchewan to give up their telephone service. Because of this, I believe that the CRTC should not allow competing long distance service by CNCP, and I urge Hon. Members to follow the wishes of thousands of Saskatchewan citizens who are indeed concerned.

subtopic: GLOBAL MILITARY EXPENDITURES-CALL FOR PARLIAMENTARY FOCUS
GLOBAL MILITARY EXPENDITURES-CALL FOR PARLIAMENTARY FOCUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the 90 seconds allowed a Member of Parliament for an opening statement, 45 children die from lack of food and medical supplies in underdeveloped parts of the world. In the same 90 seconds, over $2 million is spent on the world's military budget. Obviously if even a fraction of that amount were devoted to preserving life, many of these children would survive. The fault for this mistaken priority does not lie just with the superpowers. Six countries which could not meet their debt obligations in 1981 had spent over $1 billion each on arms imports during the previous five years. Of the world's 114 third world countries, 56 have military Governments.
To many Canadians there seems to be very little that we can do about it. That makes many of us turn all of our attention to purely national, regional, and local concerns. However, arousing the world's consciousness is vital if these disastrous priorities are to be reversed. That is something Canadians can do, especially those of us in this House. In the thirty-second Parliament an impressively large number of references to arms reduction were made by individual Members, but the same cannot be said for Parliament as a whole. Of the 591 days that Parliament sat, only two were devoted by the House as a whole to this critical challenge.
Mr. Speaker, I rise to express my indignation regarding the cruel and irresponsible character assassination of Mr. Robert Foulkes and Mr. Fred Rayer by the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson).
Hear, hear!

To make specious, unsubstantiated, and slanderous allegations about two individuals, behind the cloak of parliamentary immunity, is a shameless and cowardly act. Parliamentary immunity is a privilege of the highest order and when a Member abuses that privilege in such a cavalier fashion, it casts-

With great regret I interrupt the Hon. Member to indicate that the Member is verging on attacking another Member's use of parliamentary privilege personally. The issue of parliamentary privilege is a very careful issue. I therefore seek the Hon. Member's co-operation, in furthering the statement, to limit his concern to the issue of parliamentary privilege without personally attacking any other Hon. Member of the House.

Parliamentary immunity is a privilege of the highest order, and when a Member abuses that privilege in a cavalier fashion it casts a shadowy cloud on the integrity of each and every one of us. The purpose of parliamentary immunity is to encourage frank and full discussion, not to besmirch reputations by making capricious and ill advised statements.
The Hon. Member's inexcusable accusations have caused irreparable damage, and bring this House of Parliament into disrepute. The Member, and indeed the New Democratic Party, should hang their heads in shame. How can those self-righteous, hypocritical New Democrats-

Order, please. It does not matter one's Party. What does matter is the question of parliamentary privilege of all Members of the House. The use of the word "shame" with regard to a particular Member is out of order, I suggest. Does the Hon. Member wish to complete his statement?
It is unfortunate that the two individuals in question did not have that same privilege.

Order. I am in very great difficulty on this question. I hope Hon. Members will understand that I am. It is a very difficult situation to raise during a statement, in terms of raising a question about another Member's use of a privilege that pertains, through long standing traditions, to the rights of all Members. It is not, therefore, one that I will allow, with respect, to be continued at this time, pending some further review of the precedents on the matter by myself,
December 6, 1984

again with great respect to the Member and his concern for the issue.
The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap.

subtopic: PLIGHT OF LOGAN LAKE AREA RESIDENTS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
PLIGHT OF LOGAN LAKE AREA RESIDENTS IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago Teck Corporation closed down its Highmont Mines operation in the Highland Valley of British Columbia. As a result of that closure 450 families find themselves living in a resource town and holding lengthy mortgages with no chance of resale. To counter this problem, CMCH had entered into an agreement with Highmont Corporation, called the resource industry guarantee. Naturally, the residents of Logan Lake are anxious to receive copies of the guarantee to see what rights they have at this point.
CMHC officials have continuously stonewalled the request of residents and the Member of Parliament who has made requests on their behalf. I urge the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight), who is responsible for CMHC, to intervene in this situation to ensure that public servants actually are public servants and start to serve the residents of the Logan Lake area by making this resource industry guarantee available to them.

No, of course he didn't favour it. These were his remarks which can be of guidance to the neophyte Conservative members who are sitting in the House today silent, thinking it is a big joke. One would think that they would want to get up and participate and ensure that their Party's leadership on the front benches maintain the principle that they stood for in the last Parliament.
Here is what the Conservative finance critic said in the last Parliament on this question: "There is a well established principle that Parliament only provides sufficient borrowing authority to a government to allow it to finance its operations within the current fiscal year". That was the principle and nothing has happened to change that principle. That is a reasonable principle.
There are Conservative members in this House who are prepared to sit and make catcalls from their benches. I welcome them to join in the debate and participate. They ought to be ashamed because every time a principle is breached, the rights of Parliament are trampled on.
As a matter of fact, if the Conservatives are looking for guidance they look to their own elders in the Conservative Party. Let me quote what the Hon. Member for Yellowhead

(Mr. Clark) said. He was the former Leader of the Conservative Party. Member for Yellowhead said: "This is an affront to this Parliament. subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I rise, Mr. Speaker, to speak to the motion calling for a six-month delay in the Government's borrowing bill. It seems to me that the people of Canada, and those of my Mount Royal riding, would consider me remiss if I just said "yes" to everything, like some other Members of this House do to what the Government proposes, without having the responsibility to ask for the contract and to read the fine print. We should all read contracts and look at the fine print before we sign a blank cheque.
For example, we have heard a lot of talk about jobs, jobs, jobs, as a priority. We have had no action. We have had lots of cuts, because that is where the action seems to be centered. We have had lots of concern about cutting the deficit and about setting a climate which would incite or invite investment. With all this hyperbole about how the private sector is going to improve working conditions and do the hiring, I want to know where, when, why and how we are going to make up for those thousands and thousands of jobs presently being cut.
I want to bring to the attention of this House the remarks made by the Economic Council of Canada in its twenty-first

December 6, 1984
Borrowing Authority
annual review of the economy which was released November 27. Let me quote from it:
Putting Canadians back to work should be the Government's primary concern ... The unemployment rate is 11.3 per cent.
Mr. David Slater, the Council Chairman, said:
We must grapple now with the high rate of unemployment because it is a serious economic and social problem.
The deficit, too, needs addressing and the Government has already started bringing it under control. Reducing the Government's debt burden is important, but not sharply and suddenly with a broad axe approach to spending as some other groups would recommend.
Let me add to that "and as this Government seems to have done". The Council urged the Government to steer clear of making deep cuts in federal spending, especially on social programs. It would seem to me the Government has done exactly the opposite. We have been witness to very serious and deep cuts in all aspects of government right across the board.
I will not enumerate the size of those cuts, but I would like to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the impact that has been observed by many different groups within our society. For example, a forecasting firm, Informetrica Limited, estimated that the Government expenditure cuts and increased revenue recovery announced on November 8 by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) would result in the loss of 12,000 to
31.000	jobs. The Conference Board of Canada, another economic forecasting firm, has estimated that some 15,000 to
20.000	jobs will be lost as a result of the spending cuts.
The Government takes the position that while some jobs will be lost as a result of the decreased expenditure levels, these will be more than offset by the increased business confidence that will result from the cut-backs. I say that would be marvellous if we could be so assured, but we have no such assurance. The simple fact is that people are hungry and they are concerned. They really want to know where their next job is.
At the same time, the Minister of Finance has refused to make public the estimates carried out by his Department on the number of jobs lost as a result of the cut-backs. I think that is irresponsible on his part. Why should we have to wait for outside forecasting companies to tell us what is going to happen? Why should the Minister not be responsible to Canadians and advise them as to the impact and then say that these cuts will be made up by changes in the economic climate and the investment climate? No, Mr. Speaker, that is not what the Minister has said. He has let everybody sit back and worry. I think that is irresponsible.
The Statistics Canada leading indicator released last week indicates that a period of weaker economic growth will begin some time within the next six months. Although that may not be on the Tory calendar, nonetheless that is what is on the Tories' future slate. This does not necessarily point to the onset of a recession, and I do not wish to bring doom and gloom on to the scene, but it does tend to confirm economic forecasts indicating a slowdown in economic growth and continued high unemployment.
In this context, reduced government expenditures are not what is prescribed by the Keynesian school of economic thought and it would not find the Tories' approach very solid. I think the Keynesian school of economic thought and many forecasters in the Economic Council believe that government expenditures should contribute to increased demand in a period of sluggish growth.
To obtain an idea of how women will fare relative to men in the advent of an economic slowdown, it is useful to consider the labour market situation over the past few years. We have seen a participation rate of women of 50.4 per cent in 1980, of 51.7 per cent in 1981 and 1982, and of 52.6 per cent in 1983. Their unemployment rates went up from 8.4 per cent in 1980 to 11.6 per cent in 1983.
This data brings to the fore the fact that during the 1982 recession, women generally fared better than men in the sense that they experienced a lower unemployment rate without any decrease in their participation rate. This tends to contradict the argument that women suffer more unemployment in cyclical downturns because they are not part of the core economy.
For example, it is generally thought that women do not participate in the labour force as consistently as men because they either have to leave the labour market or hold part-time jobs because of the added burden of domestic responsibilities.
Unfortunately, women do not have that luxury today. Women work because they have to. Two incomes are needed to make ends meet. The problem is that they do not accumulate as much job seniority as men and tend to be the first to be fired in economic downturns. That this did not happen in the last recession is because the hardest hit sectors were the primary industries, manufacturing and construction, which have a predominantly male labour force.
Women participate more in the services producing industries. In particular, women are predominant in the community, business and personal services as well as the finance, insurance and real estate sectors. Thus, how women will fare in terms of job opportunities in the coming year depends largely on the performance of these sectors. However, it is difficult to ascertain how the planned cut-backs will affect these sectors relative to the goods producing sectors. In this time of changing technology, it is very important to see what the Government's policy will be and how it will affect these sectors. Only then will I be prepared to see about giving it the kind of blank cheque it wants.
Current unemployment rates for October, 1984, show that women are now experiencing higher unemployment than men, 11.6 per cent for women compared with 9.7 per cent for men. While employment for women increased by 4 per cent between October 1984 and October 1983, the female labour force increased by 4.8 per cent. Neither male employment nor the male labour force are increasing as rapidly. Do I have one more minute? Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
We are translating these percentages into 179,000 more jobs for women and 156,000 more jobs for men between October
December 6, 1984

1983 and October, 1984. To the extent that the recent cutbacks may affect the services producing industries, women may have to face higher unemployment rates in the future. I would like to be assured that the haemorrhage of job losses, which are predicated by what has happened with government cuts, is going to be controlled. Until we know that, we should not accept the borrowing Bill. We should wait until we see what is behind the blank cheque request.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a candidate in the last election, I could not help but be impressed with the commitment to political honesty and civilized behaviour that was communicated by members of the Conservative Party during that election. I understood that we differed in a number of significant respects that were cited by the Hon. Member sitting before me together with members of the Conservative Party with regard to political philosophy, but I was sure that they shared with me the concern about the cynicism generated by a pattern of hypocrisiy in politics that causes some significant questioning of what all of us share, namely a commitment to serve the Canadian people.
In view of their pronouncements during the election campaign, Members opposite are now faced with a very uncomfortable situation. They are asked to support Bill C-ll, which would communicate a strong message of inconsistency, abandonment of principles, a message that constitutes an obvious denial of a point of view which was consistently and vigorously argued upon the introduction by previous Governments of Bill C-125 and Bill C-21.
The essential and proper argument made by the then Leader of the Opposition with respect to Bill C-125, and reiterated in the motion offered by my Party and since rejected, stated then what is obvious now. What is proposed is wrong, objectionable and contravenes parliamentary practice. It is a contradiction of the principle that there should not be borrowing beyond the fiscal year.
It is worth mentioning that because of opposition resistance, the Liberals had a seizure of conscience. On both previous occasions, they withdrew the objectionable Bills. Would the Conservatives want to be seen as less respectful of this House than the Liberals were on those two previous occasions? Would they want to seem less committed to the principle of honesty than the Liberals demonstrated themselves to be on those two previous occasions?
The government Party made a number of promises during the last election campaign, promises which were broken very quickly upon their ascension to government. They broke their promises with respect to Canertech, national parks, and access to information, particularly with regard to the PetroCan takeover of Petrofina. They broke their promises with respect to taxation, research, housing and racial equality. Above all, they promised change. The kind of change they brought about is the change that one experiences on that first cold day of a winter of discontent.
I will cite two examples. With respect to culture, they assured the Canadian people that they would not do anything
Borrowing Authority
that would affect culture in Canada in a negative fashion. If one looks at what they propose to do to the cultural mandate of the CBC as it is manifest in the city of Windsor, one finds a classic example of the kind of commitment this Government has to its promises. They propose to cut $2.5 million of an $8.2 million budget for CBET, involving the dismissal of 40 people, chiefly in programming, and the abandonment of a portion of the most lucrative television newsbroadcast in the country in terms of revenue. This was proposed for a community that already experiences significant isolation. This was proposed for a community that requires something to bind it to the rest of the country, something to ensure that its Canadian identity will be continued and reinforced. This was proposed for a community in which Canada's broadcasting system represents a window away from the United States. Fortunately, the Government took pause with respect to that initiative.
On the other hand, if one looks at what has been done to young people, I suppose it would have to be mentioned that government Members promised young people very little. What they have managed to do is to provide less. They claim that they have cut $85 million from Summer Canada, a cut that would account for some 41,000 student jobs. However, they have been misleading even with respect to this claim. The fact of the matter is that the Liberal Government, in two previous fiscal years, devoted first $170 million and then $200 million to providing jobs for some 81,000 young people. This Government has not announced any substitute for that. How can we be reassured by anything that government members might say with respect to the request for borrowing authority for the next fiscal year?
There must indeed be a crisis of conscience being experienced by back-benchers who have not been exposed to the kind of cynicism that being in power generates. It must be terrible for them to have it required of them to abandon principle by seeking Parliament to give what should not have been asked for in the first place. It is time for a catharsis of conscience on the part of the government members. I would ask them to tell their leaders that they have had enough compromise and enough abandonment of principle and that they will not act in a way inconsistent with what they believe. I ask of those Conservative back-benchers who have not been committed to the cynical point of view of their leadership to tell their leaders: "No, we have had enough, we are not going to go along with this kind of abuse". Join with us and with the rest of the Opposition in supporting the hoisting of this Bill.
