speechtext:
-only just, Mr. Speaker. I see that despite the Government's massive majority, there are more Members on our side than on theirs, and I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you must feel a little uneasy about this.
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to be able to take part in this debate, and I want to thank my fellow Members for coming to the House in droves to listen to my speech. I would like to take this opportunity to point out to the House that what we are being asked to do in this Bill is, and I am sure those who know something about farming will appreciate this simile, we are being asked to buy a pig in a poke. I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lanthier) is here as part of his new duties in Parliament, and I know he is doing so at the behest of the people on the front bench when I see him violate one of the sacred principles so cherished by his fellow Members when they were in the Opposition-
I remember the debate on Bill C-125, when his colleagues claimed they were acting according to their conscience. They had a conscience at the time but they seem to be losing it now they are on the other side of the House. They are mistaken if they think this House is prepared to give them a free rein and let them spend and borrow additional funds, after what they have done to us since the beginning of this session, after the way they have cheated Canadians. Now, after only three months, the people of Canada are starting to realize this!
We saw the results of some polls today, and I think you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that it is a slow process, but after only three months they are already losing the confidence of the people of Canada. Five points, 5 per cent of Canadians have seen through this Government's game, and I am sure this is only the beginning of a general disenchantment. Imagine! Five points in three months! Mr. Speaker, it will not be long before the people of this country, before the majority of Canadians will start looking to this side of the House for other alternatives.
We must discharge our responsibilities while we wait for the next election call, Mr. Speaker, and that includes making sure that public funds are properly spent. In light of the experience we had with the economic statement and the Speech from the Throne, we have lost faith in this government and we simply cannot approve that borrowing authority until the government comes up with some kind of a program.
As you may recall, Mr. Speaker, the government was preaching virtue on the hustings, saying that Canadians would know everything, that the government would be a model of transparency. Well, Mr. Speaker, it has lost some of that transparency since the election and the opening of Parliament.
Economic and regional development is of great concern to me, so I am not prepared to issue a blank cheque. I would just like to know what their plans are before I agree to let them borrow more money. Will this additional money be used for- [English]
-"Flora's hit squad"-

Will this additional money be used to pay for the 700-man strong unemployment insurance police squad?
Hopefully not, and I am glad that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) is here, because I do hope those funds will not be used to pay those 700 people whose only goal will be to give a hard time to the most destitute Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I know that this amendment is aimed at putting off the borrowing authority for six months. I am convinced that the adoption of the amendment will enable all of us, particularly the new Members, to reflect upon what the government has been doing so far. Since the festive season is a good time to make resolutions, I hope they will take that opportunity to resolve at least to keep their promises and not to change course every time the winds shift.
With respect to youths, am I going to let the Minister of State (Youth) (Mrs. Champagne) spend God knows how many billions of dollars on behalf of young people who have no reason to complain as it is? That is what she has been saying. According to her, priority goes to young people who are doing fine. I would certainly be worried if those funds were earmarked for young people who are already fairly well off and who have no problems. I know she is saying to herself: Let us forget about the 15 per cent of those who are in a bind because there will be economic fall-outs, Mr. Speaker.
I know that Members on the other side are distressed by this situation because, in their ridings, requests for help come from young people who are experiencing difficulties, not from the others who know where the next meal is coming from.
But that does not prevent the Minister of State (Youth) (Mrs. Champagne) from telling them that she must provide help for those who have no worries because that is how the Conservative policy works.
But that is a new policy they discovered after the election, because they would never have dared to say that before!
International trade is another subject I am very much interested in. I see the Minister of External Trade (Mr. Kelleher), who travels hither and yon, and who says: We are going to spend more on export aid, on seeking out new markets-and at the same time he is cutting budgets.
Is the additional borrowing authority we are being asked to give going to be used to continue this series of contradictions, this series of broken promises?
That is why I think that we, as Parliamentarians, cannot let the Government, acting on behalf of Canadians, borrow money without knowing what it is going to do with it. I remember well the debate on C-125. It was long and it was painful, and as one of our colleagues on the left said, finally the Government, thanks to the influence of its backbenchers ... at the time backbenchers did have some influence on the Govern-
December 6, 1984

ment, while today, they all sit there without saying a word! Mr. Speaker, you have been listening to these speeches for several days, and you know that not a word has come from the Government side.
And I, especially as a Member from Quebec, $16 billion .. . and they were accusing us of not opening our mouths at the time, Mr. Speaker.
I see the Member for Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce), who spends his time speaking in his seat instead of on his feet.
Mr. Speaker, I realize they must feel uncomfortable, because they were supposed to be the great defenders of the people of Quebec. They claimed they were better than the Liberal Members, and now, they are letting themselves be run by the gang on the front bench, Mr. Speaker. 1 am thinking especially of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lanthier), who at this very moment must feel he is being used and manipulated. Asking the House for $16 billion without knowing what they want to do with it! Mr. Speaker, I wish I had a chance to ask the Parliamentary Secretary what he would do with the $16 billion. I would bet you anything he has not a clue!
Mr. Speaker, thank you for reminding me I have only two minutes left. I could spend the rest of the afternoon talking about this very serious matter of asking a responsible Parliament to turn not one but two blind eyes to what the Government is going to do with this money. I know now that many Conservative Members used to say that they were small businessmen, and that of course makes me wonder whether they were ever able to walk into the bank manager's office and apply for a loan without telling him what they would do with the money.
They kept saying that common sense would be the hallmark of their government, that everything would be crystal clear, that there would be no doubt about the course of government. Here we are debating the first major piece of legislation, for we must recall that the economic statement was supposed to be a budget, but there was no way for us to debate it directly, and so we are waiting for the real thing. If Hon. Members opposite know where they are going, Mr. Speaker, I wish they would bring down a budget in the House just so we might have a clue as to what the money is for and find out which orientation the government will follow. I know that the silent Members would like to know what their government is going to do, but their leader practically read them the riot act: Stop asking questions and come in to vote when you can, that is what counts.
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your attention and I am convinced that the longer we can put off the adoption of this measure, the clearer the conscience of Members on the other side will be.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have the opportunity to enter into this debate.
Borrowing Authority
However, I regret that we have to prolong this debate. If the Conservatives had the same sense of public principle today as they had in the summer of 1982, we would not have to extend this debate to get the argument across that what they are doing in Bill C-ll is precisely what the Liberal Government attempted to do at that time. However, the Liberal Government finally found the sense of public decency and changed; it accepted the recommendation of the Opposition and divided the Bill.
It is totally unacceptable for a government to ask for permission to borrow a certain amount in funds-inevitably from the taxpayers-for one fiscal year and then ask for an extra $16 billion for the purpose of a contingency fund.
The second thing I find distasteful is the request to borrow $23.3 billion. All we have heard from the Government since the first day of the Thirty-third Parliament is a long litany of cut-backs and termination of programs. One would have to ask the question: Why does the Government need all this money if it is going to cut back? One would have thought that the amount of money would be considerably less than the $23.3 billion which is being requested.
I want to talk about these cut-backs because the Government has indiscriminately, right across the board, cut back on virtually everything, with the possible exception of National Defence. If we listen to the longer range plans of the Government, as those plans evolve into the winter, spring and fall, I suspect that National Defence will end up spending more money in fiscal year 1985-86 than those funds which are presently allocated.
The Government wants $23.3 billion for the purpose of spending money for the balance of 1984 and for a contingency fund for 1985-86. There is something wrong. I want to bring the cuts to the attention of my constituents. I want to bring the umbrella of funding down to a basic unit, that is the constituency unit.
I happen to represent a constituency which, economically speaking, is as badly off today as it was during the depths of the recession in the summer and fall of 1982. The riding of Brant is not unlike many other constituencies, particularly those of Atlantic Canada, the remote northern areas of Canada and the interior of British Columbia, to give several examples. In the federal riding of Brant all-out war will be declared on the Unemployment Insurance Commission by the recipients of the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
It has been mentioned in fairly reliable circles that the Government will bow to the demands of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and reduce the number of benefit weeks from 52 to 26. We could imagine what would happen in a constituency such as mine, where Massey Ferguson is at the brink of disaster. There are about 1,700 employees on longterm lay-off. The company will not terminate half or even a

December 6, 1984
Borrowing Authority
third of those employees, who will probably never return to work, because if it did terminate them the company would have to pay severance pay and it does not have the money to do that.
This Government wants to include severance pay and vacation pay as declared earnings. That will hurt people on longterm lay-off. If the maximum benefit period were cut from 52 to 26 weeks it would mean that, in a riding such as mine, hundreds of men and women would be forced to go on welfare. That means the local tax base will be increased at a time when the general economy is down in my constituency and in the province, and at this time there are provinces worse off than Ontario. These are retrograde steps, giant steps backwards to the 1930s. That is what this Government is giving us. Nothing in the Conservative philosophy has changed since the days of R. B. Bennett, and we know what happened then. I predict that if this Government is determined to continue with its massive cuts and spending programs to help rejuvenate the economy, not only will it lead us into another recession but it will take us into a depression in many parts of this country.
The cut-backs in the unemployment insurance program are bad enough, but in ridings like mine where there is massive long-term unemployment, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has indicated that there is going to be the reintroduction of inspectors. They were called "Benefit Control Officers", I believe, back in the 1970s. Back in the 1970s the Government of the day decided to hire retired police officers, many of them on more than adequate pensions for that period of time, to go around and knock on doors to see if Mrs. Smith or Mr. Jones was actively searching for work. How do you actively search for work day in and day out in a city like Brantford which has a population of 75,000 and 8500 people out of work chasing some 260 jobs? How can one be expected to go out day after day, pounding on doors looking for work when there is that kind of ratio of jobs to workers? But this Government wants to force a further indignity upon the recipients of unemployment insurance benefits who will have their privacy invaded by a knock on the door by an inspector, an updated version of the Gestapo-with perhaps not the same physical tactics-asking, "When is the last time you were out looking for a job?"
It is despicable, Mr. Speaker, to think that we would go back to that time. The Conservatives across the way, along with our Party, fought this action back in the 1970s. They have now changed their minds on that. They have also changed their minds about the method of going about borrowing funds. They have forgotten the principles they espoused in 1982. Now they have come up with quasi police officers who will be checking up on those persons they suspect are not actively looking for work.
The ERDA program was basically a good one. It would take federal funding grants out of the political arena and provide moneys to industry through municipalities. It would grade municipalities according to need regardless of who its Member
of Parliament was. The former Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce had the full backing of our Party for this program. But what is the Government of the day doing, the Conservatives who supported the ERDA program? It has gutted the program by reducing its funding.
I would like to say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that we are going to hold up this legislation as long as we can to remind the Conservatives that if they had principles in the summer of 1982, they had better find those principles in the fall of 1984.

speechtext:
At least the Minister is my partner with White Shell and Chalk River.
As others have said before me, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-ll is divided into two parts. Part I asks for the authority to borrow $7.3 billion in the currrent fiscal year of 1984-1985. Part II asks for the authority to borrow $16 billion for the fiscal year 1985-1986. Many of us have sat in this House of Commons over the years and have heard the present Government-then the Opposition-shout, scream and complain about borrowing Bills, and here-a few months after Parliament has reconvened-we have a borrowing authority Bill totalling $23.3 billion. What has changed? The problem with this Bill, of course, as has already been pointed out, is that it is traditional for a government to present estimates of expenditures and revenues prior to asking for borrowing authority. This Bill is almost equal to taxation without representation.
The Conservative Government of today has not only failed to present the Estimates but it has not yet presented a budget. We on this side of the House feel that the economic statement which was delivered a few weeks ago may well be considered a budget. All we have seen so far is that "smuggled in" budget, camouflaged as an economic statement. We have studied this statement and its accompanying documents in an attempt to discern the future direction of this Government, but, believe me, Mr. Speaker, as the days go by it is becoming more and more difficult to decide in just what direction this Government is going to go.
During the last election campaign, in riding after riding across Canada, we as candidates heard our Conservative opponents say, "The day after a Conservative Government is elected, we are going to have tens of thousands of jobs". Never before, Mr. Speaker, have I had so many people lining up at my constituency office and my office here in Ottawa looking for jobs. Our Conservative opponents said as well that in order to get things done, one needed a representative on the government side of the House. And I throw that back to my hon. friend across the way. Those Hon. Members on the backbenches opposite are going to have a marvellous time before this Parliament is over because it is not just the opposition Members who are not going to have the programs to work with in the future. The programs are cut for every Member of Parliament regardless on what side of the House he or she sits. Let us stop this nonsense. We do not have to be on the government side of the House to get things done. What we need, Mr. Speaker, is a Government which has the guts, the intestinal fortitude and the humanitarianism to bring in legislation which is going to produce jobs for those people out there who are in need today.

speechtext: Right on!

speechtext:
And we did that as a government. I hear some shouting from across the way. I must be touching on some pretty sensitive nerves, Mr. Speaker. We brought in many jobs, and what did we hear during the election campaign? All
Borrowing Authority
those jobs were wasted money. In other words, those Hon. Members opposite were telling us, as they told us in this House, that money spent on human beings is wasted money. But we do not buy that as Liberals. We have compassion for those who are in need, for those who are out there looking for jobs today.
I would just like to bring to the attention of the House something which happened immediately after the last election campaign. There was an earlier agreement in place ready to be signed with the Province of Ontario. That province did not sign that agreement for months. So what happened? The money, some $75 million for forestry, was sitting there waiting for the agreement to be signed, but a few days after the Tories came into power the agreement was signed. Then what did some of the Tory Members says? It took months, they said, and the Liberals never signed an agreement with that Tory Government in Ontario. They forgot to say it was a Tory Government in Ontario but they said it only took them a few days. The only reason for that, Mr. Speaker, was that the Liberals had it already in place. It had been sitting there on the shelf and the Tories refused to come and sign it. So let us set the record straight on a number of these things.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Feel better?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Nipissing (Mr. Mantha) asks me if I feel better. I hope he feels better when some of these cuts start hitting northern Ontario. He and his colleagues are going to have to answer for them. The picnic is beginning to start. I suggest that he not shout too loudly at this point because four years is a long time.
There have been other things said here which are rather misleading, Mr. Speaker. For example, that the Liberal Government was not doing anything on defence. That is the biggest inaccuracy that could be stated. The often repeated charge that Canada was not fulfilling its commitment to NATO with respect to real growth in defence spending is simply false. The NATO commitment was 3 per cent, and this year defence spending will grow in real terms by 4.1 per cent. That is under Liberal planning and Liberal Government, but that was after we had taken $50 million out of the defence budget to put in a $307 million employment initiative program announced by our present House Leader during the campaign. If that money had been left there, we would have reached a 4.6 per cent increase in real terms in defence spending.
There is another very important point that is often overlooked or not even considered because it is hardly ever mentioned by the critics. If one were to use the NATO method of calculation, because ours is based on the gross national expenditure of the Department of Finance, Canada's performance would appear better still. It would have been over 5 per cent.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Why didn't you do it?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
We did. The Hon. Member does not know what is going on. Under NATO guidelines, Canada, as a result

December 6, 1984
Borrowing Authority
of Liberal policy, is hitting the 5 per cent mark in increased defence spending. The Hon. Member for Nipissing had better get his facts straight before he starts shouting out on the floor of this House.
Since 1974, defence spending has increased every year in real terms except during the Clark Government. In 1974-75, some $2.5 billion was spent on defence. Defence spending this year, under a Liberal budget, because this Government has not brought in a budget but simply an economic statement, will be $8.7 billion, and we projected $11.1 billion in 1986-87. At least 50 per cent of that was going into Maritime Command and on upgrading our capital equipment in the Department of National Defence.
So let us not have rumours spreading all over this land that the Tories are coming in with this great new ballgame for the Department of National Defence. We were well on our way and we have handed them an excellent program to go on. We are going to be here to see to it that they carry out those promises, bring in that extra manpower, and buy that extra equipment. As the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Coates)-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the recent election campaign we heard very little from either the then government Party, the Liberals, or from the then Official Opposition Party, the Conservatives, about the horrors of the deficit. What we heard from the then Leader of the Opposition, the current Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), was that the important issue before the people, the question that had to be answered, concerned jobs, jobs and jobs. Not only did he not worry about the deficit, but he made some 400 individual promises which the Conservatives would keep if they became the government. All of this would of course cost substantial amounts of money.
What has happened since the Government said that jobs, jobs and jobs was the issue? Now the most important, in fact the only issue facing the people of Canada is to get the deficit down.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: At any cost.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Precisely. It is pretty obvious that what the Conservative Government is doing is listening to the rhetoric of President Reagan and ignoring the reality of what he is doing. President Reagan rails against deficits and savagely cuts social programs for the poor and the needy. President Reagan endorses the idea that the U.S. should enact a constitutional amendment which would prohibit deficits at all. But the reality is that he has brought to the U.S. the biggest deficits they have ever had; much, much bigger than they were
during World War II. Indeed, the deficit in the eight years President Reagan is likely to be in office will probably amount to more than the entire deficit created in the U.S. in the almost 200 years prior to his being president. He talks about the deficit but he does not worry about it. He has improved the unemployment situation in the U.S. It is now down to the point at which it was when he was elected four years ago. He accomplished this by spending hundreds of billions of dollars on defence. That is what has fueled the recovery in the United States. What is going to fuel the economy in Canada?
This Government is cutting back on the budget by several billion dollars in the hope that the private sector will get busy and create jobs, Mr. Speaker. Why would the private sector begin to invest billions of dollars? That is what is required to put people back to work. Why would it do that when most of the major industries in this country are operating at only about 70 per cent of capacity? Private business in this country, as in any other, only operates when it can see a profit. No one can criticize it for that. If it is working at only 70 per cent capacity, there will be no major investment from the private sector.
I fear that the cuts announced by this Government so far are only the beginning. When the Prime Minister meets the premiers, I fear next February he will tell them that the funds transferred to the provinces through the Establish Programs Financing Agreements are going to be either reduced or held at the present level. That is going to mean increased expenditures and deficits for all the provincial Governments. I remind Members of Parliament, especially Conservative Members who preach about how inequitous deficits are, that every provincial Government has a deficit. Seven of those provincial Governments are Conservative. They have deficits because they are not, and should not be, prepared to make major cuts in the services which they provide for their people, and neither should the federal Government be.
We now have 11.5 per cent unemployment. Every economic research agency in the country which has looked at the prospect for the next few years has predicted that we are going to have more double digit unemployment for the next five to 10 years.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: You mean it is going to get worse?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
My hon. friend, the Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), asked if it is going to get worse. Yes, Mr. Speaker. Economists whom I have talked to, who have been much more correct over the years in their estimates of what would happen in the next year or two than the economists in the Department of Finance, have estimated that the policies of the present Government will lead to another 100,000 to 150,000 unemployed in a year from now. That is not surprising, Mr. Speaker, because the Government is more intent on reducing the deficit than it is on providing the jobs which are so necessary.
December 6, 1984

The Government talked about making our industry more efficient and more able to compete, not only in Canada but in world markets. We know from what has been done in Japan, Sweden and the United States that the way to get our industries more efficient is to invest heavily in scientific research and development. Our country has one of the worst records of all the countries that belong to the OECD. Most of the other countries are spending 2.5 per cent of Gross National Product on scientific research and development. Canada is spending substantially less than 2 per cent.
When the Conservatives were in the Opposition they joined with us and the scientific community in saying that we must do better, that we must reach 2.5 per cent of GNP invested in scientific research and development. When they got into office, however, they cut research and development funds for virtually every Department of Government. Most Canadians work in agriculture, forestry and the fishery. In every one of these fields as well as in the Government research agencies we have seen cut-backs. We have not got the details yet, but I am sure that the cuts in research will amount to tens of millions of dollars, probably to $100 million.
That means there will be cut-backs in research done in our universities. That means that our industries will become less efficient. If you look at the United States you will see that the new jobs which have been created in high technology are clustered very close to the major universities. They are in Massachusetts close to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. They are in California close to their major universities. Those universities do the basic research, and industry picks up the new techniques that it finds in those institutes and applies them in a commercial way. Instead of encouraging universities to work with industries, the Government is cutting back.
I will close, Mr. Speaker, by predicting that a year from now we will have substantially more unemployed than we have right now.

Mr. Speaker, we have had some discussions in which I have apprised my colleagues, the House Leader of the Official Opposition and the House Leader of the New Democratic Party, of the intention of the Government with respect to business of the House. I would like to inform the House that it is our intention to carry on today with Bill C-ll,
Business of the House
the borrowing authority Bill. If this Bill receives second reading today and is referred to committee, we would then enter into a discussion at the second reading stage of Bill C-12, which is a Bill relating to the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act.
It is our intention also to deal with these items tomorrow. If Bill C-ll has not passed today, we will continue with that debate tomorrow. After we finish it, if we do not manage to finish it today, we will deal with Bill C-12.
I want to designate next Monday as the final allotted day in this Supply period at which time we will, I understand, be dealing with the motion which is now on the Order Paper in the name of the Leader of the New Democratic Party. Since it will be the final Supply day, we will also want to consider at all stages the Supplementary Estimates and the Appropriation Bill.
I am pleased to announce to the House that on Tuesday we will have an opportunity to start debate, if not complete it, on a Bill relating to Investment Canada. This Bill will be introduced by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion. It is proposed that he will be introducing this Bill for first reading tomorrow. On Wednesday we hope to carry on with deliberations on that Bill and have second reading if we will not have reached it by that time.
On Wednesday I propose to call Bill C-3, the Bill relating to the courts of Ontario and Manitoba, which will be at report stage, and Bill C-5, the Bill respecting the Freshwater Fish Corporation, also at report stage. I understand that there is a disposition to deal with those two Bills on Wednesday next at report stage and third reading. In that event, if we will not yet have finished the Bill relating to Investment Canada, we can go back to that Bill on Wednesday and have some more discussion on it.
That, Mr. Speaker, is my intention for business of the House for the next week, always subject to the caveat that if circumstances change and we make progress, I would re-arrange the order to bring on further legislation. I look forward to the co-operation of the Opposition in this regard.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after reading the newspapers, watching television and listening to the radio during the last few years, I have been extremely concerned about the manner in which the House of Commons conducts its business. It seems as though the House of Commons has been paralysed by inaction when trying to solve the problems of the country. I believe that this concern is shared by the vast majority of Canadians. I also believe that among a great number of important issues in the last election, this was an issue that concerned almost every Canadian. Canadians wanted a Parliament that could get on with solving the problems of the country.
For the last few days I have listened to the debate in the House continue on with the same points being discussed over and over again. I am beginning to feel that frustration that used to well up in me, and I am sure the same frustration is being felt by many Canadians in viewing this debate during the last few days. The same points have simply been repeated over and over again.
December 6, 1984

It seems to me that there comes a time when Canadians want Members of this Parliament to deal with the pressing problems of the day. Members of the opposition Parties have spoken about pressing problems such as unemployment and problems in the economy. We were elected in order to deal with those issues. The Opposition has amended this legislation twice and I believe it has made its point very well. I believe that Canadians understand its point and I do not think it is necessary for opposition Members to keep repeating it.
I suggest that it is time to get on with the business of this country and to solve the problems of this country. If Members of the House are unable to discipline themselves to solve this problem on their own, I hope that the task force on reforming the rules of the House of Commons can solve these problems. After going through an election only three months ago, surely Hon. Members must realize that Canadians want Members of Parliament to get on with solving the problems of the country rather than simply dragging out debate endlessly for the purpose of tactics, stalling and filibustering.

Mr. Speaker, it is rather strange that a member of the Conservative Party would talk about delaying tactics in the House of Commons and about the need for the House of Commons to get down to work.
Although he is new to this place, he should know that his Party hijacked the House for days on end and weeks on end for what it believed at that time was an important principle. He should know that that Party when in opposition justified its tactical manoeuvers in this House in forwarding a principle that was important to the Canadian people. We are following in its footsteps, Mr. Speaker. We are using all of the tools that are available to us as Members of Parliament to give a message to this Government, to let this Government know that it is trampling on principles that are important to parliamentary democracy.
If the Member who has just spoken would take the time to read Hansard from the last session of Parliament, and if he were to read speeches of Members of his own Party who dealt with the matter we are dealing with today, he would see what I mean. Members from his own Party said to the Government of the day, a Liberal Government, that it was an affront to Parliament to come to the House of Commons and to ask to borrow money for the next fiscal year without any documentation on what that money was to be spent for. Those Members used every instrument available to an opposition Party in a democracy to bring the Government to its knees. They won.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Yes, we won on September 4.
Borrowing Authority

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Tories forced the Government to negotiate. My Conservative colleague says that they won on September 4. Yes, the Tories won the election on September 4, but it is rather strange that after only three months in power they should display such arrogance. They have begun to act like their Liberal counterparts who were on the other side such a short time ago. They think the only thing that matters is what happens on election day. The Tories have to keep in mind that, if they want to be in power again, they must respect this House of Commons and the people of the country.
It is important for this new Conservative Government to remain humble, to keep its feet on the ground, to remember that this country is governed by a parliamentary democracy and that one of the basic principles of a parliamentary democracy is the accountability of the executive to the Commons, and to remember that the accountability of the Government for the expenditure of money is to the representatives of the people. The Conservatives should keep in mind that some time ago another executive, a King by the name of Charles, lost his head because of this kind of action.
This Government today is losing its head. It is acting without common sense whatsoever. It is asking for money without any description of the purpose for which it wants the money. If we were to allow this Government-and the Government not think that we will allow it because we will not-to borrow money during this fiscal year for the next fiscal year without any justification, we will have the Government coming to us next year saying, "Not for the next fiscal year, but for the year after that as well".

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: They will put one Bill forward at the beginning for the entire Parliament. How ridiculous and absurd it is.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT

Absolutely, Mr. Speaker. The Tories could call this House of Commons together and bring forward a borrowing Bill that would allow them to borrow all of the money they want to spend for a four-year period, if we allowed them to get away with what they are doing now.
We hear from the back-benchers of the Conservative Party on this side that that would be a good idea. They would love just to call the House of Commons together for one sitting to pass one borrowing Bill and then go off quietly in some corner to govern the country.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: What garbage.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Conservatives are so used to being in opposition, they have had so little experience when it comes to governing, that they have to learn. Like all people, they have to learn the hard way. They have to learn that their power is not unlimited or absolute. They have to learn that their power is democratic. They can only enjoy power as long as they have the confidence of the people and as long as their actions are held accountable to the representatives of the people in this House. This means not only the representatives of the people in the Liberal Party and the NDP, but the representatives in the Conservative Party as well. It is astounding to see so many Conservative Members silent while their Cabinet, their Gov-

December 6, 1984
Borrowing Authority
ernment, arrogantly disrespects the authority of the House of Commons.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: It is the arrogance of silence.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Conservatives arrogantly disrespect the principles upon which the democratic system in this country works. It is incumbent upon every Member in this House to assert the authority of this House. The fundamental authority of this House is to hold the executive accountable for the spending of public dollars. We must and we will insist that this Government, before it gets any borrowing authority, justifies the purposes for which it seeks that borrowing authority.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives have come to us and asked us for authority to borrow $16 billion- not $16,000, not $16 million, but $16 billion. There is not one iota of description of that for which it is going to spend this money. That is utter, complete arrogance. The Conservatives have come to us without any statement of purpose for the borrowing of the money, and this is such a large sum of money. This arrogance even outdoes Liberal arrogance.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
When the Liberals were in office they came to this House and asked to borrow money for a fiscal year in the future. After a period of debate, after the Opposition brought the principle of accountability for expenditures to the House of Commons to the attention of the Liberal Government, the Liberal Government backed down. The Liberals at least backed away. But what we see now is a new level of arrogance. The Conservatives are even more arrogant in office when it comes to the spending of the public dollar than the Liberals were. Can you believe that, Mr. Speaker?
That is the Party that claims to take to heart the reform of Parliament, that claims to be the Party which respects parliamentary democracy, the Party that is tearing at the very roots and at the very principles of parliamentary democracy. I hope this Conservative Government comes to its senses. There are enough Members here who could listen to reason and could get up to speak. Why do they not go to their cabinet Ministers and say, "We will not stand for the rape of Parliament or the arbitrary spending of public dollars"? Why do these backbenchers not stand up and be counted rather than act like a group of tame sheep? We can hear them baa-ing. It would be good to hear them say something, anything, rather than the silence we get. This is an important principle. When the Conservatives were in opposition they made a number of good points as it affects this institution. Those points deserve to be respected by the Conservative Party now that it is in office. The fact that Conservatives say one thing in opposition and do another when in office breeds cynicism throughout the land. It brings into disrespect the profession of politics. It brings into disrepute every Member of the House of Commons.
I call upon this Government to wake up to its own conscience, to listen to its back-benchers who, while silent in this House, I am sure behind the curtains are counselling the Government to respect this House of Commons, to respect the
fact that the executive, the Government, is accountable for the money it spends to the elected representatives of the people.
There is no way that this borrowing authority is going to be granted to this Government. It may think that there is, but there is no way. I call upon it to enter into reasonable negotiations to find a way that respects this House of Commons and respects accountability for public expenditures. I call upon it to negotiate and come to a reasonable proposal with regard to borrowing authority.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1984-85 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I appreciate the words of the Conservative Member a few moments ago. Sometimes it appears that there is a lot of repetition and that we are almost too political in our statements in the House. Sometimes the Government does respond. A good example is something that happened a couple of days ago. I wish to congratulate one of the Conservative cabinet Ministers.
I do not want it to go to her head, but I want to mention publicly in the House of Commons-and I am sure Conservative back-benchers have done the same-that the other day the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) got approval for $6 million to try to solve the problem confronting us in part that of Newfoundland. The Minister deserves credit for listening to her opposition colleagues and members of her Party on this problem. As I said, I do not want that to go to her head because there are many other matters on which to disagree and which we will continue to raise in this House of Commons.
In my few remarks, I want to stick to the Bill before the House and to state why it should be terminated. One need not look at the major items that are under dispute. The Hon. Member said that he has not heard anything new. I went over the notes in the financial statement and the expenditure and program review of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret). I notices one small item which states that land rental rates around airports are to be automatically increased to meet a budgetary figure of $23.5 million of increased revenue through three initiatives. That does not sound like a big item. It is a minuscule part of that revenue-generating program, but it is supposed to generate considerable revenue.
This gets back to how decisions are made. What group of people inside or outside the Government have decided on specific items to increase revenues to the Government? I am sure the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) will agree that to increase land rental rates around airports violates long-standing agreements and understandings with provincial Governments and municipalities in this country. Most airport land is actually owned by provincial Governments. Through Orders in Council the provincial Governments give permission to the Ministry of Transport to operate that land for airport-related purposes. When sections of land around airports are to be used for other purposes, the consent of the provincial Government is required as well as that of the federal Government.
December 6, 1984

As the Minister of Transport knows, these agreements are usually reached on the basis of an understanding and a SI per year rental fee. Municipalities use that land in certain cases, and private industry in a lesser number of cases. Provincial government agencies are the major users for industrial parks and other purposes.
To generate revenue automatically from the lease of land that has been granted for a specific purpose violates longstanding agreements. Imagine what would happen to industrial parks around airports. They would obviously have to increase charges to users. We are talking here about provincial government agencies. If that airport uses a municipal water supply for which a set rate is paid, the municipality could well increase the charges to the federal government Department that is increasing the charges for the use of the land. It could go so far as to dispute the grants in lieu of taxes paid on airport-related buildings and properties.
It is not a simple matter of a revenue-generating source. We must consider who will be influenced. There was no consultation with the provincial Governments before this decision was taken. I am sure of that. It was handed down from on high to be initiated by the Minister of Transport. The transportation commitment of this Government given in Halifax, Nova Scotia, on August 2, 1984, was to accelerate the construction of airport and other federal transport-related projects. All we see in the financial statements are cuts and increased revenue generated from the leasing of those facilities.
At the same meeting on August 2, the Government announced that a fund would be set up to finance the cost of a submarine cable between the mainland and the Island of Newfoundland. I do not see the cost of a cable from Labrador to Newfoundland in this financial statement. I do not see it in any statement made after this Party came to power. A cable is needed. You have to do something. You cannot put it over the Gulf of St. Lawrence because that would be an awfully big bridge. You cannot put it on top of the water because that would damage shipping. I suppose you could put it under the straits. That was tried. This is why I raise the matter today.
We saw the history of this commitment over television a few years ago in Newfoundland. A Conservative Government announced it would put a cable under that section of the Atlantic Ocean. It said it would build a tunnel through which cars as well as the cable could pass through. They even set off the blasts, both at the same time, one on the mainland and one on the Island. The television cameras were there to record the big explosions. The holes are still in the ground. The Conservative Party still has not given up on its promise. That is exactly what it is, a promise.
There is no mention of a cable in the financial papers. The cable will go the same route as the tunnel. It is just a promise. I could go on to list 380 other reasons for stopping the present legislation from being passed by the House.
